paras: The attempted lynching of Matthew Lewis and Jesse Ray was an assault by a mob of about forty men on the jail at Springfield, Washington County, Kentucky, early on Sunday, August 11, 1895. The mob got the jail keys but could not open the cells, fired into them without hitting anyone, and left; the sheriff then moved both men to Louisville. Papers across the country ran the story because the would-be lynchers were said to have been too drunk to unlock the doors.

Lewis and Ray, described as Black, were charged with a criminal assault on Mrs. Murray Shields, "a white woman," on the Monday before the attack. A Lebanon dispatch of August 9 reported that Sheriff Simms of Washington County had left Lebanon the night before with Lewis, and that "his arrival in Washington county will be followed by a lynching."

About 1 a.m. on August 11 the mob came to the Springfield jail and demanded the keys to the prisoners' cells. The jailer, "seeing resistance was useless," handed them over. According to the wire account, everyone in the mob was drunk and none could work the locks, so they brought sledge hammers and tried to batter down the doors, giving up after two hours (one copy says an hour).

The men then emptied their revolvers into the cells, but no one was hit. A separate Lebanon dispatch, which does not mention drink, said they marched around the jail shooting into the windows, "hoping in this way to kill the negroes." They returned the keys and told the jailer they would be back that night. The mob was said to be made up of men from Washington and Marion counties, nine of them from Lebanon.

The Washington County sheriff took Lewis and Ray through Lebanon to Louisville that day, and a Louisville dispatch named him as Sheriff Craycroft and said the prisoners were lodged in the county jail. The same dispatch said that had they stayed at Springfield "they would surely have been lynched." No report of arrests of the mob, or of a trial of the two prisoners, appears in the coverage.

On August 26 a smaller mob hanged Harrison Lewis, accused of killing Joe Brooks, in the Springfield courthouse yard; the Washington Evening Star described him as Matthew Lewis's brother and recalled that Matthew had "narrowly escaped lynching" two weeks earlier.

The story spread through a special from Lebanon to the Louisville Commercial, reprinted from Utah to West Virginia between August 12 and 16. Headlines made a joke of the failure: "LYNCHING AVERTED. Mob Was Too Full," "WENT HOME TO SOBER UP," "DRUNKEN LYNCHERS. They Took Too Much Booze, and Missed Their Prey," and "A Little Entertainment Didn't Come Off."

Most versions stated the accusation as fact, saying the men "outraged Mrs. Shields, white." The Fort Worth Gazette called the attackers "a Savage Mob," while the Coconino Sun called the prisoners "two negro brutes" and the Southern Christian Advocate called them "ravishers." Kentucky papers in Maysville and Stanford ran their own short accounts, and no Black-press coverage of the attempt was found.

The Stanford Interior Journal placed the attack on Saturday night and named the second prisoner "Jackson Ray," while other copies give Jess or James. The sheriff who moved Lewis is called Simms in one dispatch and Craycroft in another.

bases: A mob of about forty men seized the jail keys at Springfield, Ky., to hang two Black prisoners accused of assault and fired into their cells, but failed to reach them (A2, A11, A13).
About forty men acting without authority tried to hang two prisoners accused of assaulting a white woman, but no one was killed or hit (A2, A11, A13); it was an attempted lynching.

The Lebanon wire to the Louisville Commercial (A2, A3, A11) and the separately written Maysville Ledger and Stanford Interior Journal accounts (A12, A13) agree on the mob, the failed break-in and the removal to Louisville.
